title: Pass-Through Variable
pattern: A variable that is passed down through a long chain of intermediate functions or methods that have no use for the variable themselves, only forwarding it to a low-level call.
why_bad: It clutters signatures and couples intermediate layers to low-level parameters that they should not care about. It makes the system highly resistant to change: adding a new low-level configuration parameter requires modifying every interface along the entire path.
detection: An argument in a function signature that is passed directly to another function call without being read, validated, or transformed locally, occurring recursively across multiple nested call frames.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Generic wrappers or context-passing structures in frameworks where general-purpose parameters must traverse standard handlers.
fix: Group the parameter into an existing shared context/configuration object, or introduce a dependency injection container, or refactor the top-level code to call the low-level utility directly, bypassing intermediate layers.
source: John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Chapter 7 ("Different Layer, Different Abstraction - Pass-Through Variables"), pp. 46, 314–315.
